answers.pearl: Autonomic arousal and anxiety during withdrawal can produce hyperventilation.

answers.name: Severe anemia
answers.pearl: Reduced oxygen delivery and carotid body stimulation modestly increase ventilation.

answers.name: Heat stroke
answers.pearl: Hyperthermia and increased respiratory drive cause hyperventilation early in heat illness.

answers.name: Hepatopulmonary syndrome
answers.pearl: Intrapulmonary vascular dilatation causes hypoxemia and orthodeoxia, which stimulate ventilation.

answers.name: Cheyne-Stokes respiration
answers.pearl: Heart failure and brain injury cause periodic breathing with hyperventilatory phases and hypocapnia.

answers.name: Brainstem lesion
answers.pearl: Tegmental or pontine lesions can cause sustained central neurogenic hyperventilation.

answers.name: Doxapram
answers.pearl: A respiratory stimulant that acts on peripheral chemoreceptors and the medulla to increase ventilation.

answers.name: Voluntary hyperventilation
answers.pearl: Deliberate or habitual overbreathing rapidly lowers PaCO2 and ionized calcium, causing tingling and carpopedal spasm.

answers.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
answers.pearl: Early ARDS often shows hyperventilation from hypoxemia and lung receptor stimulation before fatigue sets in.

answers.name: Hypovolemic shock
answers.pearl: Hypoperfusion and chemoreceptor stimulation raise minute ventilation before lactic acidosis dominates.

answers.name: Sarcoidosis
answers.pearl: Parenchymal involvement and hypoxemia stimulate respiration; hypocapnia is common until end-stage fibrosis.

answers.name: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
answers.pearl: Alveolar inflammation and hypoxemia increase respiratory drive, with low PaCO2.

answers.name: Acute chest syndrome
answers.pearl: Pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxemia in sickle cell disease cause tachypnea and hypocapnia.

answers.name: Progesterone therapy
answers.pearl: Medroxyprogesterone stimulates the respiratory center and lowers PaCO2.

answers.name: Lymphangitic carcinomatosis
answers.pearl: Tumor infiltration of lung lymphatics causes dyspnea, hypoxemia and tachypnea with hypocapnia.

answers.name: Dinitrophenol toxicity
answers.pearl: Uncouplers of oxidative phosphorylation cause hyperthermia and marked hyperventilation, with metabolic acidosis in advanced poisoning.

answers.name: Urea cycle disorders
answers.pearl: Hyperammonemia in neonates with OTC deficiency or citrullinemia directly stimulates respiration, producing respiratory alkalosis.

answers.name: Joubert syndrome
answers.pearl: Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia with the molar tooth sign causes episodic tachypnea alternating with apnea in infancy.

answers.name: Rett syndrome
answers.pearl: MECP2 mutations cause breathing irregularities with episodic hyperventilation and breath-holding.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of hypercapnia (respiratory acidosis).
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Tick paralysis and Pompe disease (rare but documented); Sodium oxybate/GHB and baclofen (CNS depression, overdose data); Carbohydrate overfeeding (modest in current practice); Hypermagnesemia; Compensation for metabolic alkalosis (physiologic rather than pathologic); CO2 inhalation from dry ice or silos; Thoracoplasty (historic). Board Prep Traps: malignant hyperthermia, Ondine curse, and Prader-Willi.

answers.name: COPD exacerbation
answers.pearl: Worsening airflow obstruction, dead space and respiratory muscle fatigue cause CO2 retention in chronic bronchitis and emphysema.

answers.name: Opioid overdose
answers.pearl: Mu-opioid receptors in the brainstem reduce respiratory drive, producing hypoventilation and rapid CO2 retention.

answers.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
answers.pearl: Chest wall loading, blunted leptin-driven respiratory drive and sleep-disordered breathing cause daytime hypercapnia.

answers.name: Benzodiazepine overdose
answers.pearl: Sedatives depress ventilatory drive, especially when combined with opioids or alcohol.

answers.name: Severe asthma
answers.pearl: Normal or rising PaCO2 during an asthma attack indicates fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

answers.name: Sleep apnea
answers.pearl: Obstructive events cause recurrent hypoventilation, and untreated severe cases can lead to chronic daytime hypercapnia.

answers.name: Pneumonia
answers.pearl: Severe consolidation with exhaustion or underlying lung disease can cause hypercapnic failure.

answers.name: Myasthenia gravis
answers.pearl: Respiratory muscle weakness in crisis reduces ventilation, and an FVC under 20 mL/kg predicts the need for ventilation.

answers.name: Guillain-Barre syndrome
answers.pearl: Ascending demyelinating polyneuropathy causes diaphragmatic weakness, with serial FVC and NIF monitoring.

answers.name: Upper airway obstruction
answers.pearl: Foreign body, epiglottitis or angioedema prevents effective ventilation.

answers.name: ALS
answers.pearl: Motor neuron loss weakens the diaphragm and ventilatory failure is the usual cause of death.

answers.name: Pulmonary edema
answers.pearl: Alveolar flooding with fatigue can produce hypercapnic failure in severe cases.

answers.name: Pneumothorax
answers.pearl: Large or tension pneumothorax causes ventilatory failure with rising PaCO2.

answers.name: Oxygen therapy in COPD
answers.pearl: Excess supplemental oxygen can worsen V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect, raising PaCO2 in chronic retainers.

answers.name: Stroke
answers.pearl: Brainstem infarction or hemorrhage can impair central respiratory drive.

answers.name: Kyphoscoliosis
answers.pearl: Severe chest wall deformity restricts ventilation and causes chronic hypercapnia.

answers.name: Rib fractures
answers.pearl: Pain with flail segments splints breathing and impairs ventilation.

answers.name: Cystic fibrosis
answers.pearl: Progressive obstructive and bronchiectatic disease causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch and chronic respiratory failure.

answers.name: Muscular dystrophy
answers.pearl: Progressive respiratory muscle weakness leads to nocturnal and then daytime hypoventilation.

answers.name: General anesthesia
answers.pearl: Volatile and intravenous agents depress ventilation, and residual neuromuscular blockade worsens hypercapnia.

answers.name: Alcohol intoxication
answers.pearl: Ethanol depresses respiratory drive and impairs airway protection.

answers.name: Cervical spinal cord injury
answers.pearl: Injury above C3-C5 disrupts phrenic nerve output and causes diaphragmatic paralysis.

answers.name: Respiratory muscle fatigue
answers.pearl: Excessive work of breathing eventually exhausts the diaphragm, and PaCO2 rises as tachypnea fades.

answers.name: Permissive hypercapnia
answers.pearl: Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS or asthma accepts higher PaCO2 to limit barotrauma.

answers.name: Neuromuscular blockade
answers.pearl: Paralytics or residual blockade eliminate respiratory effort unless ventilation is supported.

answers.name: Large pleural effusion
answers.pearl: Massive effusion restricts lung expansion and chest wall mechanics.

answers.name: Interstitial lung disease
answers.pearl: End-stage fibrosis can lead to ventilatory failure when muscle fatigue develops.

answers.name: Compensation for metabolic alkalosis
answers.pearl: The respiratory center reduces ventilation to retain CO2 and offset elevated bicarbonate.

answers.name: Hypothyroidism
answers.pearl: Myxedema coma reduces respiratory drive and muscle strength, causing hypoventilation.

answers.name: Diaphragm paralysis
answers.pearl: Bilateral phrenic palsy or paralysis causes orthopnea, hypoxemia and CO2 retention.

answers.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
answers.pearl: Early panacinar emphysema leads to chronic airflow obstruction and hypercapnia.

answers.name: Massive pulmonary embolism
answers.pearl: Large clot burden raises physiologic dead space, and respiratory failure with high PaCO2 may appear in arrest or fatigue.

answers.name: Status epilepticus
answers.pearl: Convulsions and postictal depression cause hypoventilation and mixed acidosis.

answers.name: Botulism
answers.pearl: Presynaptic acetylcholine blockade causes descending paralysis including respiratory muscles.

answers.name: Organophosphate poisoning
answers.pearl: Cholinesterase inhibition causes bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, and respiratory muscle paralysis.

answers.name: Central sleep apnea
answers.pearl: Disordered central drive in heart failure, opioid use or brainstem lesions leads to hypoventilation.

answers.name: Hypermagnesemia
answers.pearl: Excess magnesium blocks neuromuscular transmission and causes loss of reflexes and respiratory paralysis.

answers.name: Laparoscopic CO2 insufflation
answers.pearl: Peritoneal CO2 absorption and diaphragmatic splinting raise PaCO2 during laparoscopic surgery.

answers.name: Baclofen overdose
answers.pearl: GABA-B agonism depresses CNS and respiratory drive, including during intrathecal pump malfunction or withdrawal.

answers.name: Sodium oxybate
answers.pearl: GHB or sodium oxybate causes dose-related respiratory depression, particularly when combined with other sedatives.

answers.name: Spinal muscular atrophy
answers.pearl: Anterior horn cell degeneration weakens intercostal and diaphragm muscles, causing hypoventilation.

answers.name: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
answers.pearl: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause proximal weakness and occasionally respiratory failure.

answers.name: Pompe disease
answers.pearl: Acid maltase deficiency causes glycogen storage in the diaphragm, with respiratory failure out of proportion to limb weakness.

answers.name: Tick paralysis
answers.pearl: A neurotoxin from engorged Dermacentor ticks causes ascending paralysis that resolves after tick removal.

answers.name: Primary alveolar hypoventilation
answers.pearl: Idiopathic loss of automatic ventilatory control causes hypercapnia that worsens in sleep with normal lungs.

answers.name: Malignant hyperthermia
answers.pearl: Hypermetabolism with rising end-tidal CO2 is an early sign, after volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine exposure; treat with dantrolene.

answers.name: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
answers.pearl: PHOX2B mutations cause failure of automatic breathing in sleep, historically called Ondine's curse.

answers.name: Prader-Willi syndrome
answers.pearl: Hypothalamic dysfunction, obesity and blunted ventilatory response lead to sleep-related hypoventilation.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of hypernatremia.
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Essential hypernatremia and adipsic hypernatremia (rare, described in series); Gestational diabetes insipidus (rare); Cidofovir (nephrogenic DI, limited reports); Munchausen by proxy salt poisoning (forensic cases); SGLT2 inhibitors (osmotic diuresis, usually minor); Overcorrection of hyponatremia (iatrogenic water loss after treatment). Board Prep Traps: Langerhans cell histiocytosis and Wolfram syndrome.

answers.name: Dehydration
answers.pearl: Water loss exceeds intake, so plasma tonicity rises, most often in elderly or bedbound patients with inadequate free water access.

answers.name: Diabetes insipidus
answers.pearl: Absent or ineffective ADH produces dilute high-volume urine, and hypernatremia develops if thirst or access to water fails.

answers.name: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
answers.pearl: The collecting duct is resistant to ADH from lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia and inherited defects.

answers.name: Diarrhea
answers.pearl: GI fluid loss, particularly osmotic diarrhea, is relatively low in sodium and so concentrates the plasma.

answers.name: Osmotic diuresis
answers.pearl: Glucose, mannitol or urea in the tubule drive water loss in excess of sodium.

answers.name: Loop diuretics
answers.pearl: Loop diuretics impair concentrating ability and cause excess water loss relative to sodium in some settings.

answers.name: Fever
answers.pearl: Insensible water loss from skin and respiration increases with temperature and tachypnea.

answers.name: Burns
answers.pearl: Evaporative losses from burned skin are high in free water, and resuscitation fluid choice affects sodium.

answers.name: Impaired thirst
answers.pearl: Dementia, delirium, sedation and stroke reduce thirst or the ability to ask for water.

answers.name: Vomiting
answers.pearl: Gastric fluid loss with poor intake contributes to hypernatremic dehydration.

answers.name: Hypertonic saline
answers.pearl: Infusion of concentrated sodium without matching water raises serum sodium quickly.

answers.name: Lithium
answers.pearl: Lithium downregulates aquaporin-2 channels and causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus in a large fraction of long-term users.

answers.name: Sodium bicarbonate administration
answers.pearl: Sodium bicarbonate solutions deliver a large sodium load, particularly with repeated boluses in cardiac arrest.

answers.name: Hypercalcemia
answers.pearl: High calcium impairs ADH action in the collecting duct and causes nephrogenic DI.

answers.name: Heat stroke
answers.pearl: Heavy sweating loses hypotonic fluid, and thirst and access to water are limited.

answers.name: Enteral tube feeding
answers.pearl: High-solute formulas without enough free water cause hypertonic dehydration.

answers.name: Traumatic brain injury
answers.pearl: Hypothalamic or pituitary injury can cause central DI, typically within days of the injury.

answers.name: Pituitary surgery
answers.pearl: Transsphenoidal surgery can cause transient or permanent central DI, sometimes with a triphasic pattern.

answers.name: Mannitol
answers.pearl: Osmotic diuretics cause water loss and raise plasma osmolality.

answers.name: Laxatives
answers.pearl: Osmotic laxatives such as lactulose cause hypotonic stool losses.

answers.name: Brain death
answers.pearl: Loss of hypothalamic ADH production leads to central DI with massive polyuria in organ donors.

answers.name: Infant formula mixing errors
answers.pearl: Over-concentrated formula delivers excess solute and sodium to infants.

answers.name: Hypokalemia
answers.pearl: Low potassium impairs concentrating ability and aquaporin-2 expression, leading to polyuria.

answers.name: Primary hyperaldosteronism
answers.pearl: Mild hypernatremia can occur from sodium retention, with hypokalemia and hypertension.

answers.name: Salt poisoning
answers.pearl: Ingestion of salt, seawater or salt-containing emetics delivers a large sodium load.

answers.name: Cushing syndrome
answers.pearl: Glucocorticoid excess, with mineralocorticoid effects, can cause mild hypernatremia.

answers.name: Sickle cell disease
answers.pearl: Medullary infarction impairs urinary concentration (hyposthenuria), causing nephrogenic DI.

answers.name: Recovery phase of acute tubular necrosis
answers.pearl: Polyuria in the diuretic phase can cause hypernatremia if free water is not replaced.

answers.name: Postobstructive diuresis
answers.pearl: Large solute and water losses after relief of obstruction can overshoot.

answers.name: Craniopharyngioma
answers.pearl: Suprasellar tumors and their resection can cause central DI and hypothalamic thirst disorders.

answers.name: High-sodium intravenous antibiotics
answers.pearl: Carbenicillin, ticarcillin and some penicillins carry a large sodium load.

answers.name: Amphotericin B
answers.pearl: Amphotericin damages the distal tubule and causes concentrating defects.

answers.name: Demeclocycline
answers.pearl: Tetracyclines inhibit ADH effect at the collecting duct, causing nephrogenic DI.

answers.name: Hemodialysis with high-sodium dialysate
answers.pearl: Excess dialysate sodium transfers sodium to the patient during treatment.

answers.name: Cystic fibrosis
answers.pearl: Sweat losses of salt and water, plus poor intake and diarrhea, can cause hypernatremia.

answers.name: Overcorrection of hyponatremia
answers.pearl: Aquaresis after cessation of ADH stimulus (for example after treating hypovolemia or stopping thiazide) can overshoot the target.

answers.name: Sjogren syndrome
answers.pearl: Interstitial nephritis and distal RTA cause concentrating defects.

answers.name: Amyloidosis
answers.pearl: Medullary amyloid deposition produces nephrogenic DI.

answers.name: Foscarnet
answers.pearl: Foscarnet causes nephrogenic DI and tubular injury.

answers.name: Hypothalamic lesions
answers.pearl: Lesions of the osmoreceptors cause adipsic hypernatremia where thirst fails despite hyperosmolality.

answers.name: Sarcoidosis
answers.pearl: Hypothalamic or pituitary stalk granulomas cause central DI, and hypercalcemia can add nephrogenic DI.

answers.name: Cidofovir
answers.pearl: Cidofovir causes proximal tubular toxicity and can induce nephrogenic DI.

answers.name: Gestational diabetes insipidus
answers.pearl: Placental vasopressinase degrades ADH, causing transient DI late in pregnancy.

answers.name: AVPR2 mutation
answers.pearl: X-linked nephrogenic DI from a defective V2 receptor presents in infancy in boys.

answers.name: AQP2 mutation
answers.pearl: Aquaporin-2 mutations cause autosomal nephrogenic DI, with ADH failing to open water channels.

answers.name: AVP-neurophysin II mutation
answers.pearl: Autosomal dominant familial central DI from AVP-NPII mutations causes progressive neuronal degeneration.

answers.name: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
answers.pearl: Granulomatous infiltration of the pituitary stalk causes central diabetes insipidus.

answers.name: Wolfram syndrome
aliases: diabetes insipidus diabetes mellitus optic atrophy deafness
answers.pearl: WFS1 mutations cause DIDMOAD: diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy and deafness.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of erythrocytosis (polycythemia, elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit).
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Meningioma (ectopic EPO, case-report level); Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (EPO production, small series); Cushing syndrome (mild, inconsistent); Dengue plasma leakage (hemoconcentration rather than true erythrocytosis); Hydronephrosis (rare renal EPO excess); Cobalt toxicity (arthroplasty case reports); Uterine leiomyoma. Chuvash polycythemia, Gaisbock syndrome (disputed entity) and cerebellar hemangioblastoma scored as Board Prep Traps.

answers.name: Dehydration
answers.pearl: Plasma volume contraction raises hematocrit without any increase in red cell mass (relative erythrocytosis) and normalizes with rehydration.

answers.name: Polycythemia vera
answers.pearl: A JAK2-driven myeloproliferative neoplasm with a low erythropoietin level and a high risk of thrombosis.

answers.name: Smoking
answers.pearl: Chronic carboxyhemoglobinemia lowers oxygen delivery and drives a compensatory EPO rise, and smoking also contracts plasma volume.

answers.name: COPD
answers.pearl: Chronic hypoxemia in advanced obstructive lung disease increases erythropoietin secretion.

answers.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
answers.pearl: Recurrent nocturnal hypoxemia stimulates EPO production, although the effect on hematocrit is usually modest.

answers.name: High altitude
answers.pearl: Low inspired oxygen tension increases HIF-mediated EPO production as a physiologic adaptation.

answers.name: Testosterone therapy
answers.pearl: Exogenous testosterone raises hematocrit in a dose-dependent way, especially with injectable formulations.

answers.name: Cyanotic congenital heart disease
answers.pearl: Right-to-left shunting causes chronic arterial hypoxemia and a secondary erythrocytosis.

answers.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
answers.pearl: Chronic daytime hypercapnia with hypoxemia produces secondary erythrocytosis.

answers.name: Renal cell carcinoma
answers.pearl: Tumor cells can overproduce erythropoietin, causing paraneoplastic erythrocytosis in a minority of patients.

answers.name: Hepatocellular carcinoma
answers.pearl: Ectopic erythropoietin secretion by hepatomas is a classic paraneoplastic cause.

answers.name: Anabolic steroids
answers.pearl: Androgenic steroids stimulate erythropoiesis directly and via increased EPO.

answers.name: Diuretics
answers.pearl: Chronic diuretic use contracts plasma volume and can cause a relative erythrocytosis.

answers.name: Erythropoietin abuse
answers.pearl: Exogenous EPO or ESAs used for blood doping raise hemoglobin and viscosity, a risk in endurance athletes.

answers.name: Interstitial lung disease
answers.pearl: Chronic hypoxemia from fibrosing lung disease stimulates erythropoietin production.

answers.name: Carbon monoxide exposure
answers.pearl: Chronic carboxyhemoglobin impairs oxygen delivery and triggers compensatory EPO release; pulse oximetry is falsely reassuring.

answers.name: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors
answers.pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors raise EPO and cause osmotic diuresis, producing a consistent small rise in hematocrit.

answers.name: Polycystic kidney disease
answers.pearl: Cyst-related interstitial hypoxia leads to inappropriate EPO production, in contrast with the anemia of most CKD.

answers.name: Eisenmenger syndrome
answers.pearl: Reversed shunt flow from pulmonary hypertension causes chronic hypoxemia with erythrocytosis, and phlebotomy is only for symptomatic hyperviscosity.

answers.name: Severe burns
answers.pearl: Early plasma loss from burns causes marked hemoconcentration and a spuriously elevated hematocrit.

answers.name: Renal artery stenosis
answers.pearl: Renal hypoperfusion can drive excess EPO production by the affected kidney.

answers.name: Hydronephrosis
answers.pearl: Obstructive uropathy causes renal tissue hypoxia and inappropriate EPO secretion in rare cases.

answers.name: Post-transplant erythrocytosis
answers.pearl: Occurs in about 10 to 15 percent of kidney transplant recipients, mediated by the native kidneys and angiotensin II, and responds to ACE inhibitors.

answers.name: Central or neuromuscular hypoventilation
answers.pearl: Chronic alveolar hypoventilation from neuromuscular disease or central disorders causes sustained hypoxemia and secondary polycythemia.

answers.name: Cushing syndrome
answers.pearl: Chronic hypercortisolism raises red cell mass modestly and can cause a plethoric appearance.

answers.name: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation
answers.pearl: Right-to-left shunting across pulmonary AVMs, classically in HHT, produces hypoxemia and erythrocytosis.

answers.name: Chronic mountain sickness
answers.pearl: Excessive erythrocytosis in long-term high-altitude residents, with hypoxemia, headache and pulmonary hypertension.

answers.name: Capillary leak syndrome
answers.pearl: Plasma extravasation during attacks raises hematocrit sharply, and it is usually seen with a monoclonal gammopathy (Clarkson disease).

answers.name: Dengue with plasma leakage
answers.pearl: The critical phase of dengue features plasma leakage, and a rising hematocrit is the hallmark that warns of shock.

answers.name: Uterine leiomyoma
answers.pearl: Rare fibroids secrete erythropoietin and cause erythrocytosis that resolves with hysterectomy.

answers.name: HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors
answers.pearl: Roxadustat and similar agents stabilize HIF to raise EPO, and overshoot of hemoglobin is a recognized adverse effect.

answers.name: Pheochromocytoma
answers.pearl: Rare catecholamine-secreting tumors may produce EPO or cause hemoconcentration from vasoconstriction.

answers.name: High oxygen affinity hemoglobin variant
answers.pearl: Variants such as Hb Chesapeake hold oxygen tightly, producing tissue hypoxia and a compensatory rise in EPO.

answers.name: Cobalt toxicity
answers.pearl: Cobalt stabilizes HIF and has caused erythrocytosis in patients with failing metal-on-metal hip prostheses.

answers.name: EPOR gain-of-function mutation
answers.pearl: Truncating mutations of the EPO receptor cause primary familial and congenital polycythemia with low EPO and sustained JAK2 signaling.

answers.name: Meningioma
answers.pearl: Rare reported cases of EPO-secreting meningiomas have normalized hematocrit after resection.

answers.name: PHD2 (EGLN1) mutation
answers.pearl: Loss-of-function variants in the prolyl hydroxylase that degrades HIF cause familial erythrocytosis with inappropriately normal or high EPO.

answers.name: HIF-2 alpha (EPAS1) gain-of-function mutation
answers.pearl: Stabilizing EPAS1 variants cause familial erythrocytosis and predispose to paraganglioma.

answers.name: 2,3-BPG mutase deficiency
answers.pearl: Reduced 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate raises hemoglobin oxygen affinity and thus causes tissue hypoxia and erythrocytosis.

answers.name: Pacak-Zhuang syndrome
answers.pearl: The triad of polycythemia, paraganglioma and somatostatinoma arises from somatic or mosaic EPAS1 gain-of-function.

answers.name: Chuvash polycythemia
answers.pearl: Homozygous VHL R200W mutation impairs HIF degradation, raising EPO and VEGF; a classic board entity.

answers.name: Gaisbock syndrome
answers.pearl: Stress or spurious polycythemia in hypertensive, obese, middle-aged men, probably reflecting low plasma volume.

answers.name: Cerebellar hemangioblastoma
answers.pearl: Hemangioblastomas in von Hippel-Lindau disease or sporadically secrete EPO and cause erythrocytosis.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of rhabdomyolysis.
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Haff disease and quail poisoning (regional, mechanism incompletely defined); Tricholoma equestre mushroom (French/Polish case series); TANGO2 deficiency (recent genetic entity); Immune checkpoint inhibitors (myositis more than frank rhabdomyolysis); Mitochondrial myopathy and RYR1 variants (episodic, genetically heterogeneous). McArdle disease, CPT II deficiency and malignant hyperthermia scored as Board Prep Traps.

answers.name: Crush injury
answers.pearl: Direct muscle trauma releases myoglobin, CK and potassium, and aggressive early fluids are key to preventing kidney injury.

answers.name: Statins
answers.pearl: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors cause myopathy and rarely rhabdomyolysis, with risk raised by CYP3A4 inhibitors, fibrates and hypothyroidism.

answers.name: Strenuous exercise
answers.pearl: Unaccustomed or extreme exertion (marathons, CrossFit, military training) can cause exertional rhabdomyolysis, especially with heat and dehydration.

answers.name: Alcohol
answers.pearl: Binge intake causes direct myotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia and prolonged immobility.

answers.name: Cocaine
answers.pearl: Cocaine causes vasoconstriction, agitation, hyperthermia and seizures, and it is one of the most frequent drug causes.

answers.name: Prolonged immobilization
answers.pearl: Being down for hours after a fall, intoxication or overdose compresses muscle and produces ischemic injury (the long lie).

answers.name: Seizures
answers.pearl: Prolonged convulsive activity causes sustained muscle contraction, hyperthermia and energy depletion.

answers.name: Amphetamines
answers.pearl: Stimulants such as methamphetamine and MDMA produce hyperthermia, agitation and vasoconstriction.

answers.name: Heat stroke
answers.pearl: Core temperatures above 40 C denature muscle proteins and cause direct myocyte injury.

answers.name: Hypokalemia
answers.pearl: Severe potassium depletion impairs the vasodilatory response of exercising muscle and causes necrosis.

answers.name: Viral infection
answers.pearl: Influenza, coxsackie, EBV and others can cause myositis with rhabdomyolysis, particularly in children and during influenza epidemics.

answers.name: Sepsis
answers.pearl: Systemic infection, hypotension and cytokine-mediated injury contribute to muscle necrosis.

answers.name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
answers.pearl: Dopamine blockade (or withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy) causes rigidity, fever, autonomic instability and markedly elevated CK.

answers.name: Opioid or drug overdose
answers.pearl: Overdose with sedatives or opioids causes prolonged compression of muscle on hard surfaces, often with hypoxia.

answers.name: Compartment syndrome
answers.pearl: Raised compartment pressure causes ischemic muscle necrosis, and fasciotomy is the treatment.

answers.name: Fibrates
answers.pearl: Gemfibrozil in particular reduces statin glucuronidation and raises statin exposure, thereby markedly increasing myotoxicity.

answers.name: Hypophosphatemia
answers.pearl: Depletion of intracellular ATP impairs membrane integrity, as seen in refeeding syndrome and alcohol withdrawal.

answers.name: Electrical injury
answers.pearl: High-voltage injury and lightning cause deep muscle necrosis that exceeds the visible skin burn.

answers.name: Limb ischemia and reperfusion
answers.pearl: Arterial occlusion or tourniquet use followed by reperfusion releases myoglobin and potassium (myonephropathic metabolic syndrome).

answers.name: Hypothyroidism
answers.pearl: Thyroid hormone deficiency reduces muscle energy metabolism and lowers the threshold for statin or exertional injury.

answers.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
answers.pearl: Severe hyperglycemic crises cause hypophosphatemia, electrolyte shifts and hyperosmolarity that predispose to muscle breakdown.

answers.name: COVID-19
answers.pearl: SARS-CoV-2 infection has been associated with myalgia, very high CK values and frank rhabdomyolysis.

answers.name: Hypothermia
answers.pearl: Cold exposure with shivering, immobility and vasoconstriction can lead to rhabdomyolysis.

answers.name: Bariatric surgery positioning
answers.pearl: Prolonged surgery in morbidly obese patients leads to gluteal and paraspinal muscle compression injury, a classic perioperative form.

answers.name: Serotonin syndrome
answers.pearl: Excess serotonergic activity causes clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia and elevated CK.

answers.name: Sickle cell trait
answers.pearl: Extreme exertion, heat and dehydration cause red cell sickling with muscle ischemia, an important cause of death in athletes and military recruits.

answers.name: Polymyositis
answers.pearl: Inflammatory myopathies occasionally present with CK values high enough to cause myoglobinuria.

answers.name: Pyomyositis
answers.pearl: Bacterial infection of skeletal muscle, typically Staphylococcus aureus, can cause local necrosis and rhabdomyolysis.

answers.name: Propofol infusion syndrome
answers.pearl: High-dose, prolonged propofol interferes with mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and causes rhabdomyolysis, acidosis, and cardiac failure.

answers.name: Colchicine
answers.pearl: Colchicine myotoxicity is more likely in renal impairment or with CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors such as clarithromycin.

answers.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
answers.pearl: Hypoxic muscle injury and prolonged immobilization from CO poisoning can both produce rhabdomyolysis.

answers.name: Daptomycin
answers.pearl: Daptomycin can cause myopathy with CK elevation, and the risk rises when it is combined with statins or in renal impairment.

answers.name: Succinylcholine
answers.pearl: The depolarizing muscle relaxant can trigger hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis in patients with undiagnosed myopathy such as Duchenne dystrophy.

answers.name: Snake envenomation
answers.pearl: Sea snake and some viper and elapid bites cause myotoxicity, and Russell's viper envenomation also produces rhabdomyolysis.

answers.name: Dystrophinopathy
answers.pearl: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are susceptible to exertional or anesthetic-triggered rhabdomyolysis.

answers.name: Immune checkpoint inhibitors
answers.pearl: Checkpoint inhibitors cause myositis, sometimes with myocarditis and myasthenia, and CK may be extreme.

answers.name: Necrotizing autoimmune myopathy
answers.pearl: Anti-HMGCR or anti-SRP antibodies cause persistent proximal weakness with very high CK, even after the statin is stopped.

answers.name: Mitochondrial myopathy
answers.pearl: Defective oxidative phosphorylation reduces energy supply and can precipitate episodic rhabdomyolysis with fasting, infection or exercise.

answers.name: Very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
answers.pearl: A fatty acid oxidation defect that can present in adults with exercise- or fasting-induced rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria.

answers.name: RYR1 variant
answers.pearl: Pathogenic RYR1 variants cause exertional rhabdomyolysis and heat intolerance, even without a malignant hyperthermia history.

answers.name: Lipin-1 deficiency
answers.pearl: LPIN1 mutations are the most common genetic cause of recurrent rhabdomyolysis in children, triggered by fever or fasting.

answers.name: Haff disease
answers.pearl: Unexplained rhabdomyolysis occurring within hours of eating certain freshwater or buffalo fish, presumably from an unidentified toxin.

answers.name: Quail poisoning
answers.pearl: Coturnism follows eating quail that fed on hemlock, causing myalgia and rhabdomyolysis.

answers.name: Tricholoma equestre mushroom
answers.pearl: Repeated ingestion of this mushroom (the man-on-horseback) has caused fatal rhabdomyolysis in several case series.

answers.name: TANGO2 deficiency
answers.pearl: A recently described disorder presenting with metabolic crises, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia and encephalopathy.

answers.name: McArdle disease
answers.pearl: Myophosphorylase deficiency causes exercise intolerance, second-wind phenomenon and rhabdomyolysis with no lactate rise.

answers.name: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
answers.pearl: The most common inherited cause of recurrent myoglobinuria in adults, triggered by prolonged exercise, fasting or cold.

answers.name: Malignant hyperthermia
answers.pearl: Volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine trigger uncontrolled sarcoplasmic calcium release (RYR1) causing hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis; treat with dantrolene.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of nephrotic syndrome (primary and secondary).
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Castleman disease/TAFRO (case-report level); Coenzyme Q10 deficiency and LCAT deficiency (rare genetic proteinuric disease); Allergic triggers such as bee stings (anecdotal minimal change); Tiopronin; Leprosy omitted; Schistosomiasis and quartan malaria (regional, mainly historical); IgG4-related disease (membranous pattern); Immune checkpoint inhibitors (mostly minimal change/ATIN case series). Finnish-type congenital nephrotic syndrome, Nail-patella syndrome and Fabry disease scored as Board Prep Traps.

answers.name: Diabetic nephropathy
answers.pearl: The most common cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria in adults, with nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson glomerulosclerosis.

answers.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
answers.pearl: A leading primary cause in adults, especially in Black patients with APOL1 risk variants, and often steroid-resistant.

answers.name: Membranous nephropathy
answers.pearl: A common primary cause in adults, usually due to anti-PLA2R antibodies, with subepithelial deposits and spike-and-dome appearance.

answers.name: Minimal change disease
answers.pearl: The classic cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and is steroid-responsive, with effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy.

answers.name: Lupus nephritis
answers.pearl: Class V lupus nephritis in particular causes nephrotic syndrome, and diffuse proliferative disease may also.

answers.name: NSAIDs
answers.pearl: NSAIDs can cause minimal change disease or membranous nephropathy, usually with concomitant interstitial nephritis.

answers.name: Amyloidosis
answers.pearl: AL or AA amyloid deposits cause heavy proteinuria and may spare the typical nephritic features; Congo red shows apple-green birefringence.

answers.name: Hepatitis B
answers.pearl: HBV causes membranous nephropathy (especially in children in endemic areas) and MPGN.

answers.name: HIV-associated nephropathy
answers.pearl: Collapsing FSGS with microcystic tubular dilation in patients of African ancestry with uncontrolled HIV.

answers.name: Hepatitis C
answers.pearl: HCV is associated with MPGN, often with cryoglobulinemia, and occasionally membranous nephropathy.

answers.name: Hodgkin lymphoma
answers.pearl: A classic secondary cause of minimal change disease, which may precede or follow the lymphoma diagnosis.

answers.name: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
answers.pearl: Immune-complex or complement-mediated disease with tram-track basement membrane duplication, often presenting with mixed nephritic and nephrotic features.

answers.name: Solid tumor
answers.pearl: Carcinoma of the lung, breast, colon, prostate, or stomach can cause secondary membranous nephropathy through tumor-antigen immune complexes.

answers.name: IgA nephropathy
answers.pearl: Some patients with IgA disease (and minimal change overlap) have nephrotic-range proteinuria.

answers.name: Multiple myeloma
answers.pearl: Light-chain amyloid, light-chain deposition disease or monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance can cause nephrotic syndrome, but cast nephropathy usually does not.

answers.name: Obesity-related glomerulopathy
answers.pearl: Hyperfiltration from increased body mass causes secondary FSGS with proteinuria that is often sub-nephrotic.

answers.name: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis
answers.pearl: Poststreptococcal GN can occasionally present with nephrotic-range proteinuria in addition to the nephritic syndrome.

answers.name: Syphilis
answers.pearl: Secondary syphilis causes membranous nephropathy, which responds to penicillin.

answers.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
answers.pearl: Nephrotic syndrome in RA is usually from secondary AA amyloidosis or from treatment with gold or penicillamine.

answers.name: Gold or penicillamine
answers.pearl: These disease-modifying drugs cause membranous nephropathy, which usually resolves after discontinuation.

answers.name: Reflux nephropathy
answers.pearl: Chronic vesicoureteral reflux with scarring causes adaptive secondary FSGS.

answers.name: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis
answers.pearl: Reduced nephron mass and glomerular hypertension cause secondary FSGS, though proteinuria is usually non-nephrotic.

answers.name: Sickle cell nephropathy
answers.pearl: Chronic hyperfiltration and ischemia cause secondary FSGS and proteinuria that often responds to ACE inhibition.

answers.name: Heroin nephropathy
answers.pearl: A form of FSGS in intravenous heroin users, now rarely seen, with possible contribution from infection.

answers.name: Bisphosphonates
answers.pearl: High-dose pamidronate classically causes collapsing FSGS, and zoledronate less so.

answers.name: Interferon
answers.pearl: Interferon alfa, beta and gamma therapy causes minimal change disease or collapsing FSGS.

answers.name: Lithium
answers.pearl: Chronic lithium use can cause minimal change disease or FSGS in addition to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

answers.name: Captopril
answers.pearl: ACE inhibitor captopril, particularly at high dose, has historically been associated with membranous nephropathy.

answers.name: Cryoglobulinemia
answers.pearl: Type II mixed cryoglobulinemia, usually from HCV, causes MPGN with nephrotic proteinuria.

answers.name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
answers.pearl: CLL can cause membranous nephropathy, MPGN, or minimal change disease.

answers.name: Infective endocarditis
answers.pearl: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis can cause nephrotic-range proteinuria in addition to hematuria.

answers.name: Schistosomiasis
answers.pearl: Schistosoma mansoni causes immune-complex glomerulopathy (often MPGN or FSGS) in endemic areas.

answers.name: Quartan malaria
answers.pearl: Plasmodium malariae causes immune-complex nephropathy and nephrotic syndrome that is poorly responsive to steroids.

answers.name: APOL1-associated nephropathy
answers.pearl: High-risk APOL1 genotypes in persons of West African ancestry drive FSGS and collapsing glomerulopathy, including COVID-19 associated cases.

answers.name: Sarcoidosis
answers.pearl: Rarely causes nephrotic syndrome through membranous nephropathy or MCD, apart from granulomatous interstitial nephritis.

answers.name: Sjogren syndrome
answers.pearl: Primary Sjogren disease is more typically associated with interstitial nephritis, but membranous nephropathy and MPGN are reported.

answers.name: Anti-VEGF therapy
answers.pearl: Bevacizumab and other VEGF pathway inhibitors cause proteinuria and glomerular thrombotic microangiopathy.

answers.name: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis
answers.pearl: Randomly arranged 15 to 25 nm fibrils that are Congo red negative and DNAJB9 positive cause nephrotic syndrome.

answers.name: Immune checkpoint inhibitors
answers.pearl: Rarely, immunotherapy triggers minimal change disease or other podocytopathies in addition to tubulointerstitial nephritis.

answers.name: NELL-1 associated membranous nephropathy
answers.pearl: A PLA2R-negative membranous subtype that is associated with malignancy, lipoic acid, mercury-containing skin lighteners and kratom.

answers.name: Thrombospondin type-1 domain-containing 7A membranous nephropathy
answers.pearl: THSD7A-positive membranous nephropathy is a less common target antigen and is associated with malignancy in a subset.

answers.name: Immunotactoid glomerulopathy
answers.pearl: Microtubular organized deposits with larger fibrils (greater than 30 nm), often with underlying lymphoproliferative disease.

answers.name: Coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis defects
answers.pearl: COQ2, COQ6 and related mutations cause early-onset steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, and CoQ10 supplementation can help.

answers.name: Pierson syndrome
answers.pearl: LAMB2 mutation causes congenital nephrotic syndrome with microcoria and neurologic abnormalities.

answers.name: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type
answers.pearl: Nephrin (NPHS1) mutation causes massive proteinuria in infancy, with dramatic edema and a large placenta.

answers.name: Nail-patella syndrome
answers.pearl: LMX1B mutation produces dysplastic nails, absent patellae, iliac horns and a glomerulopathy with basement membrane lucency.

answers.name: Fabry disease
answers.pearl: X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes podocyte and tubular glycosphingolipid accumulation with proteinuria; zebra bodies are seen on EM.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of a hypercoagulable state or thrombophilia.
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Elevated factor XI (epidemiologic association); Dysfibrinogenemia (usually bleeding, thrombotic subset); Heparin cofactor II deficiency (weak thrombotic evidence); Tissue plasminogen activator deficiency and elevated PAI-1 or TAFI (impaired fibrinolysis, modest evidence); Hypereosinophilic syndrome; Vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (associated with adenoviral vaccines). Homocystinuria, Trousseau syndrome and PNH scored as Board Prep Traps. MTHFR polymorphisms deliberately excluded (not an established cause).

answers.name: Malignancy
answers.pearl: Cancer (especially pancreatic, gastric, lung and ovarian) activates coagulation through tissue factor and mucin expression.

answers.name: Factor V Leiden
answers.pearl: The most common inherited thrombophilia, caused by activated protein C resistance, and more common in people of European ancestry.

answers.name: Pregnancy
answers.pearl: Rising procoagulant factors, falling protein S, venous stasis and delivery trauma raise VTE risk, which peaks in the postpartum period.

answers.name: Estrogen-containing contraceptives
answers.pearl: Combined oral contraceptives, patches and rings raise levels of procoagulant factors and acquired protein S and antithrombin deficits.

answers.name: Antiphospholipid syndrome
answers.pearl: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies cause arterial and venous thrombosis, with pregnancy loss.

answers.name: Surgery
answers.pearl: Operations, especially orthopedic and abdominal-pelvic, cause endothelial injury, stasis and a postoperative inflammatory response.

answers.name: Immobilization
answers.pearl: Venous stasis from bed rest, casts, paralysis or long travel leads to thrombosis.

answers.name: Prothrombin gene mutation
answers.pearl: The G20210A variant increases prothrombin levels and is the second most common inherited thrombophilia.

answers.name: Nephrotic syndrome
answers.pearl: Urinary loss of antithrombin and proteins C and S together with hepatic synthesis of procoagulants and hyperviscosity.

answers.name: Obesity
answers.pearl: Adipose tissue promotes inflammation, elevated PAI-1 and factor VIII levels, and venous stasis.

answers.name: Protein C deficiency
answers.pearl: Reduced inactivation of Va and VIIIa predisposes to VTE and also warfarin-induced skin necrosis.

answers.name: Protein S deficiency
answers.pearl: A cofactor for protein C and TFPI is reduced; levels fall in pregnancy, estrogen use and acute thrombosis, which complicates testing.

answers.name: Antithrombin deficiency
answers.pearl: Antithrombin III deficiency is the most thrombogenic inherited defect and may cause heparin resistance.

answers.name: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
answers.pearl: Antibodies against PF4-heparin complexes activate platelets and cause arterial and venous thrombosis despite thrombocytopenia.

answers.name: Central venous catheter
answers.pearl: Intravascular devices cause endothelial injury and local flow disturbance, leading to catheter-related thrombosis.

answers.name: Polycythemia vera
answers.pearl: Increased red cell mass and viscosity as well as JAK2-driven platelet and leukocyte activation lead to thrombosis, including splanchnic thrombosis.

answers.name: Essential thrombocythemia
answers.pearl: Elevated platelet counts and leukocyte activation (JAK2, CALR, MPL) cause both thrombosis and paradoxical bleeding.

answers.name: Hormone replacement therapy
answers.pearl: Oral estrogen with or without progestin increases the risk of VTE, with the transdermal route carrying lower risk.

answers.name: COVID-19
answers.pearl: SARS-CoV-2 causes endothelial injury, inflammation, and microvascular and macrovascular thrombosis.

answers.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
answers.pearl: Active Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis increase thrombosis through inflammatory activation and platelet and fibrinogen abnormalities.

answers.name: Heart failure
answers.pearl: Venous stasis, low flow and inflammatory activation increase the risk of both venous thromboembolism and intracardiac thrombus.

answers.name: Hyperhomocysteinemia
answers.pearl: Elevated homocysteine from B-vitamin deficiency or renal failure promotes endothelial injury and thrombosis, though lowering it hasn't reduced events.

answers.name: Trauma
answers.pearl: Tissue factor release, endothelial injury and immobility give a high risk after major trauma and spinal cord injury.

answers.name: Sepsis
answers.pearl: Systemic inflammation and tissue factor expression cause hypercoagulability and consumption, with microvascular thrombosis.

answers.name: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
answers.pearl: Widespread thrombin generation leads to microthrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors.

answers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
answers.pearl: Lupus patients have a higher risk of thrombosis, particularly with antiphospholipid antibodies and nephritis.

answers.name: Elevated factor VIII
answers.pearl: High factor VIII levels, partly genetic and partly from inflammation, are an independent risk factor for VTE and for recurrence.

answers.name: Tamoxifen
answers.pearl: Selective estrogen receptor modulators such as tamoxifen and raloxifene cause a two- to threefold increase in VTE risk.

answers.name: Testosterone therapy
answers.pearl: Exogenous testosterone raises the hematocrit and has been linked to increased venous thromboembolism.

answers.name: Sickle cell disease
answers.pearl: Chronic hemolysis, endothelial activation and a loss of the usual procoagulant balance create a hypercoagulable state.

answers.name: Tranexamic acid
answers.pearl: Antifibrinolytic agents increase thrombotic risk, particularly in patients with other risk factors.

answers.name: Behcet disease
answers.pearl: Vasculitis with endothelial dysfunction causes venous thrombosis, including Budd-Chiari syndrome and cerebral venous thrombosis.

answers.name: Lenalidomide or thalidomide
answers.pearl: Immunomodulatory agents cause VTE, especially when combined with dexamethasone in multiple myeloma.

answers.name: Asparaginase
answers.pearl: Asparaginase lowers antithrombin and fibrinogen synthesis, leading to a high risk of cerebral venous and other thromboses in ALL regimens.

answers.name: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
answers.pearl: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes platelet-rich microthrombi in small vessels, with microangiopathic hemolysis.

answers.name: JAK inhibitors
answers.pearl: Tofacitinib and similar agents carry a boxed warning for venous thromboembolism.

answers.name: Hyperviscosity syndrome
answers.pearl: Elevated paraprotein levels in Waldenstrom or myeloma slow flow and raise thrombotic risk.

answers.name: Vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia
answers.pearl: Anti-PF4 antibodies after adenoviral vector COVID-19 vaccines cause cerebral venous and splanchnic thromboses with thrombocytopenia.

answers.name: Elevated factor XI
answers.pearl: Higher factor XI levels are associated with a modestly higher VTE risk, which is a rationale for factor XI inhibitor drugs.

answers.name: Dysfibrinogenemia
answers.pearl: Some structural fibrinogen variants form abnormally resistant clots or impair fibrinolysis and cause thrombosis.

answers.name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome
answers.pearl: Eosinophil-derived tissue factor and endothelial damage cause arterial and venous thrombosis.

answers.name: Elevated PAI-1
answers.pearl: Impaired fibrinolysis from high plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 contributes to thrombosis in obesity and metabolic syndrome.

answers.name: Heparin cofactor II deficiency
answers.pearl: A thrombin inhibitor that is deficient in some thrombosis families, but the clinical association is weak.

answers.name: Thrombomodulin variants
answers.pearl: Rare mutations in the endothelial thrombomodulin gene cause impaired protein C activation and venous thrombosis in a few families.

answers.name: Tissue plasminogen activator deficiency
answers.pearl: Reduced tPA release is a rare cause of impaired fibrinolysis and recurrent thrombosis.

answers.name: Homocystinuria
answers.pearl: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency causes marfanoid habitus, lens dislocation, intellectual disability and early thromboembolism.

answers.name: Trousseau syndrome
answers.pearl: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis as a harbinger of occult visceral malignancy, classically pancreatic cancer.

answers.name: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
answers.pearl: A PIGA mutation causes complement-mediated hemolysis and venous thrombosis, often at unusual sites such as hepatic or cerebral veins.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of pulmonary hypertension.
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (vasculopathy, rare); Gaucher disease (mechanism uncertain); Glycogen storage disease type I (small series); Toxic rapeseed oil (historical epidemic); Alveolar capillary dysplasia (neonatal); Tumor thrombotic microangiopathy; Left atrial myxoma; Pulmonary artery sarcoma (usually misdiagnosed as CTEPH). Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, Schistosomiasis and Fenfluramine scored as Board Prep Traps.

answers.name: Left heart failure
answers.pearl: Elevated left atrial pressure passively raises pulmonary venous and arterial pressure, making it the most common cause worldwide (group 2).

answers.name: COPD
answers.pearl: Chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling cause group 3 pulmonary hypertension in emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

answers.name: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
answers.pearl: Persistent organized thrombi obstruct the pulmonary arteries (group 4), and it is diagnosed with V/Q scan and potentially curable by endarterectomy.

answers.name: Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension
answers.pearl: A rare, progressive pulmonary arteriopathy of unknown cause that mostly affects young women (group 1).

answers.name: Interstitial lung disease
answers.pearl: Fibrosis, destruction of vascular bed and hypoxia combine to cause group 3 disease, and it carries a poor prognosis.

answers.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
answers.pearl: Recurrent nocturnal hypoxemia and intrathoracic pressure swings produce mild pulmonary hypertension.

answers.name: Systemic sclerosis
answers.pearl: Both pulmonary arterial hypertension and interstitial lung disease occur in scleroderma, especially limited disease with anti-centromere antibodies.

answers.name: Mitral stenosis
answers.pearl: Obstruction at the mitral valve raises left atrial pressure and thus pulmonary venous pressure (group 2).

answers.name: Acute pulmonary embolism
answers.pearl: A sudden obstruction raises pulmonary vascular resistance and causes acute right ventricular strain.

answers.name: Congenital heart disease with shunt
answers.pearl: Left-to-right shunts such as ASD, VSD and PDA expose the pulmonary bed to excess flow, with eventual Eisenmenger syndrome.

answers.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
answers.pearl: Chronic hypercapnia and hypoxemia induce pulmonary vasoconstriction.

answers.name: Portal hypertension
answers.pearl: Portopulmonary hypertension occurs in a small percentage of cirrhotics and counts as group 1 disease.

answers.name: Sickle cell disease
answers.pearl: Chronic hemolysis, nitric oxide scavenging and recurrent chest syndromes contribute, and a tricuspid regurgitant velocity above 2.5 m/s predicts mortality.

answers.name: HIV infection
answers.pearl: HIV-associated PAH is a group 1 etiology, probably caused by chronic inflammation and viral proteins.

answers.name: Aortic stenosis
answers.pearl: Elevated left ventricular filling pressure from severe aortic valve disease leads to postcapillary pulmonary hypertension.

answers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
answers.pearl: Connective tissue disease-associated PAH, as well as interstitial lung disease and recurrent PE with antiphospholipid antibodies.

answers.name: Mitral regurgitation
answers.pearl: Chronic or acute severe regurgitation raises left atrial pressure and thus pulmonary pressures.

answers.name: High altitude
answers.pearl: Chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction at altitude raises pulmonary pressure, and it can cause high-altitude pulmonary edema in the susceptible.

answers.name: Sarcoidosis
answers.pearl: Granulomas, fibrosis, extrinsic compression by lymph nodes and vasculopathy can all cause pulmonary hypertension (group 5).

answers.name: Mixed connective tissue disease
answers.pearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a leading cause of death in MCTD, with anti-U1 RNP positivity.

answers.name: Methamphetamine use
answers.pearl: Stimulant exposure is a definite risk factor for PAH, histologically indistinguishable from idiopathic disease.

answers.name: Heritable PAH
answers.pearl: BMPR2 mutations are present in most heritable cases and in a subset of apparently idiopathic ones, with incomplete penetrance.

answers.name: Cystic fibrosis
answers.pearl: Advanced lung disease with hypoxemia and fibrosis produces group 3 pulmonary hypertension.

answers.name: Chronic kidney disease
answers.pearl: Volume overload, dialysis access fistulae, and endothelial dysfunction contribute, and the condition is common in dialysis patients (group 5).

answers.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
answers.pearl: Failure of the normal postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance causes right-to-left shunting at the ductus and foramen ovale.

answers.name: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
answers.pearl: Disrupted alveolar and vascular development in preterm infants causes lasting pulmonary hypertension.

answers.name: Dasatinib
answers.pearl: This tyrosine kinase inhibitor causes reversible PAH in some patients and it often improves after the drug is stopped.

answers.name: Thalassemia
answers.pearl: Chronic hemolysis, splenectomy, iron overload and a hypercoagulable state increase pulmonary pressures (group 5).

answers.name: Intravenous drug use with talc granulomatosis
answers.pearl: Injected insoluble excipients from crushed oral tablets lodge in the pulmonary vasculature and cause granulomas and pulmonary hypertension.

answers.name: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis
answers.pearl: Cystic lung disease with vasculopathy causes severe pulmonary hypertension in smokers.

answers.name: Myeloproliferative neoplasms
answers.pearl: Essential thrombocythemia, polycythemia vera and myelofibrosis can cause group 5 PH via thrombosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis and other mechanisms.

answers.name: Pulmonary vein stenosis
answers.pearl: Stenosis after atrial fibrillation ablation or as a congenital disorder obstructs pulmonary venous return and raises pulmonary pressures.

answers.name: Fibrosing mediastinitis
answers.pearl: Histoplasma-associated fibrosis can encase and compress the pulmonary arteries and veins.

answers.name: Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease
answers.pearl: Postcapillary obstruction causes pulmonary edema with a normal wedge pressure and a low DLCO, with vasodilators risking pulmonary edema.

answers.name: Takayasu arteritis
answers.pearl: Large-vessel vasculitis can involve the pulmonary arteries and cause obstruction or stenosis.

answers.name: Left atrial myxoma
answers.pearl: A pedunculated tumor can obstruct mitral inflow and raise left atrial pressure, mimicking mitral stenosis.

answers.name: Pulmonary artery sarcoma
answers.pearl: A rare intimal sarcoma obstructs pulmonary artery flow and is often misdiagnosed as chronic thromboembolic disease.

answers.name: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
answers.pearl: Cystic lung disease in women with TSC or sporadic LAM can be complicated by pulmonary hypertension.

answers.name: Behcet disease
answers.pearl: Pulmonary artery aneurysms and thrombosis cause obstructive hypertension; anticoagulation risks hemoptysis in aneurysm.

answers.name: Neurofibromatosis type 1
answers.pearl: NF1 vasculopathy and lung disease can produce severe pulmonary hypertension, usually in women.

answers.name: Gaucher disease
answers.pearl: Glucocerebroside-laden macrophages and plugging of the vasculature are reported, and it is classified in group 5.

answers.name: Glycogen storage disease type I
answers.pearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a known complication, possibly through serotonin and endothelial dysfunction.

answers.name: Tumor thrombotic microangiopathy
answers.pearl: Tumor emboli cause widespread occlusion of small pulmonary arteries and rapidly progressive pulmonary hypertension, most commonly from gastric cancer.

answers.name: Toxic rapeseed oil syndrome
answers.pearl: Adulterated oil caused an epidemic in Spain in 1981 that was followed by persistent pulmonary hypertension in some survivors.

answers.name: Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins
answers.pearl: FOXF1 variants cause a lethal neonatal disorder with refractory pulmonary hypertension and misaligned veins.

answers.name: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
answers.pearl: ENG and ACVRL1 (ALK1) mutations cause PAH that is clinically identical to heritable PAH, in addition to pulmonary AVMs.

answers.name: Schistosomiasis
answers.pearl: Egg embolization to the pulmonary arterioles in hepatosplenic disease causes a plexiform arteriopathy, a leading cause worldwide.

answers.name: Fenfluramine
answers.pearl: Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine anorexigens cause valvulopathy and PAH, historically known as the fen-phen epidemic.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of hypoxemia.
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Exercise-induced diffusion limitation in elite athletes (physiologic, not disease); Paraquat poisoning; Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis; Primary ciliary dyskinesia (hypoxemia only in advanced disease); Venous air embolism and Amniotic fluid embolism (acute, case-based); Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (HHT-related). Methemoglobinemia and carbon monoxide poisoning deliberately excluded (low saturation without low PaO2). Platypnea-orthodeoxia, Hepatopulmonary syndrome and Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome scored as Board Prep Traps.

answers.name: Pneumonia
answers.pearl: Alveolar consolidation causes intrapulmonary shunt and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

answers.name: COPD
answers.pearl: Airflow obstruction and emphysematous destruction cause V/Q mismatch, often with CO2 retention during exacerbations.

answers.name: Pulmonary embolism
answers.pearl: Perfusion is blocked to ventilated lung, creating dead space and V/Q mismatch, and it may open a right-to-left shunt through a PFO.

answers.name: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
answers.pearl: The most common mechanism of hypoxemia, which corrects with supplemental oxygen.

answers.name: Pulmonary edema
answers.pearl: Fluid in the alveoli from cardiogenic or noncardiogenic causes impairs gas exchange and causes shunt.

answers.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
answers.pearl: Diffuse alveolar damage causes refractory hypoxemia from shunt, and it responds poorly to oxygen alone.

answers.name: Asthma
answers.pearl: Bronchospasm and mucus plugging cause V/Q mismatch, and severe attacks produce hypoxemia.

answers.name: Right-to-left shunt
answers.pearl: Blood bypasses ventilated alveoli, whether intracardiac or intrapulmonary, and hypoxemia fails to correct with 100 percent oxygen.

answers.name: Atelectasis
answers.pearl: Collapsed alveoli are perfused but not ventilated, a common form of postoperative hypoxemia.

answers.name: Pneumothorax
answers.pearl: A collapsed lung with continued perfusion causes shunt, and tension pneumothorax also impairs venous return.

answers.name: Pleural effusion
answers.pearl: Compressive atelectasis from large effusions leads to V/Q mismatch.

answers.name: Hypoventilation
answers.pearl: Reduced alveolar ventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PaO2 with a normal A-a gradient.

answers.name: Low inspired oxygen
answers.pearl: Low FiO2 at altitude, in smoke-filled spaces or from gas supply failure lowers alveolar PO2 with a normal A-a gradient.

answers.name: Opioid overdose
answers.pearl: Respiratory center depression causes hypoventilation and hypoxemia.

answers.name: Interstitial lung disease
answers.pearl: Fibrosis thickens the alveolar-capillary membrane and causes V/Q mismatch, with exertional desaturation prominent.

answers.name: Aspiration
answers.pearl: Gastric contents or food cause pneumonitis, obstruction and atelectasis.

answers.name: COVID-19
answers.pearl: Viral pneumonitis and endothelial dysfunction can produce profound hypoxemia, even with minimal dyspnea (happy hypoxia).

answers.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
answers.pearl: Reduced chest wall compliance and blunted ventilatory drive cause chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia.

answers.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
answers.pearl: Recurrent upper airway collapse causes repetitive nocturnal oxygen desaturations.

answers.name: Congenital cyanotic heart disease
answers.pearl: Right-to-left intracardiac shunts as in tetralogy of Fallot or transposition cause hypoxemia that does not correct with oxygen.

answers.name: Upper airway obstruction
answers.pearl: Epiglottitis, laryngospasm, tumors, tracheal stenosis or foreign bodies block ventilation entirely.

answers.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
answers.pearl: Diffuse alveolar disease in immunocompromised patients causes profound exertional desaturation, as seen with HIV.

answers.name: Neuromuscular disease
answers.pearl: Respiratory muscle weakness in conditions such as ALS, myasthenia gravis or Guillain-Barre causes hypoventilation.

answers.name: Rib fractures
answers.pearl: Splinting, pain and flail chest impair ventilation and cause atelectasis and contusion.

answers.name: Acute chest syndrome
answers.pearl: Sickle cell vaso-occlusion in the lung, infection and fat embolism cause new infiltrates and hypoxemia.

answers.name: Drug-induced lung disease
answers.pearl: Amiodarone, bleomycin, nitrofurantoin and methotrexate can cause pneumonitis and fibrosis.

answers.name: Fat embolism
answers.pearl: Long-bone fracture releases marrow fat that causes pulmonary vascular obstruction and inflammation with petechiae and confusion.

answers.name: Pneumoconiosis
answers.pearl: Occupational dust such as asbestos, silica or coal produces progressive fibrosis.

answers.name: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
answers.pearl: Alveolar bleeding from capillaritis, anticoagulation or Goodpasture disease fills the alveoli with blood and produces rapid hypoxemia.

answers.name: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation
answers.pearl: Abnormal arteriovenous connections, classically in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, create an anatomic right-to-left shunt that does not correct with oxygen.

answers.name: Mainstem intubation
answers.pearl: Advancing the endotracheal tube into one bronchus leaves the other lung unventilated but perfused.

answers.name: Diaphragmatic paralysis
answers.pearl: Phrenic nerve injury causes hypoxemia, particularly when supine, from basal atelectasis and hypoventilation.

answers.name: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
answers.pearl: Surfactant accumulation (GM-CSF antibodies) in the alveoli causes shunt, and the lavage fluid is milky.

answers.name: Lymphangitic carcinomatosis
answers.pearl: Tumor in pulmonary lymphatics produces interstitial thickening and diffusion impairment.

answers.name: Re-expansion pulmonary edema
answers.pearl: Rapid evacuation of a large effusion or pneumothorax causes unilateral edema from capillary stress failure.

answers.name: Transfusion-related acute lung injury
answers.pearl: Donor antibodies cause noncardiogenic pulmonary edema within six hours of transfusion.

answers.name: Neurogenic pulmonary edema
answers.pearl: A catecholamine surge after subarachnoid hemorrhage or seizure causes capillary leak.

answers.name: Negative-pressure pulmonary edema
answers.pearl: Forceful inspiration against an obstructed airway (laryngospasm) generates large negative intrathoracic pressure and alveolar flooding.

answers.name: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
answers.pearl: Smooth muscle proliferation and cysts in women with TSC or sporadic disease lead to progressive hypoxemia and pneumothoraces.

answers.name: Primary ciliary dyskinesia
answers.pearl: Impaired mucociliary clearance (Kartagener syndrome) leads to bronchiectasis and chronic hypoxemia.

answers.name: Amniotic fluid embolism
answers.pearl: Peripartum anaphylactoid reaction causes sudden hypoxemia, cardiovascular collapse and DIC.

answers.name: Venous air embolism
answers.pearl: Air entering the venous circulation during central line placement or surgery causes right-sided obstruction, V/Q mismatch and sudden hypoxemia.

answers.name: Paraquat poisoning
answers.pearl: Herbicide ingestion causes progressive pulmonary fibrosis and refractory hypoxemia, and oxygen therapy worsens injury.

answers.name: Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis
answers.pearl: Calcium phosphate microliths fill the alveoli (SLC34A2 mutation), producing a sandstorm appearance on radiograph.

answers.name: Exercise-induced diffusion limitation
answers.pearl: In elite endurance athletes high cardiac output shortens red cell transit time and causes arterial desaturation at maximal exercise.

answers.name: Platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome
answers.pearl: Hypoxemia and dyspnea that worsen upright and improve supine, from shunting across a PFO or pulmonary AVMs.

answers.name: Hepatopulmonary syndrome
answers.pearl: Intrapulmonary vascular dilatation in advanced liver disease produces shunt and hypoxemia that worsens upright, and is diagnosed with a bubble echo.

answers.name: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
answers.pearl: PHOX2B mutations cause failure of autonomic control of breathing, leading to hypoventilation during sleep (Ondine curse).

prompts.prompt: Name causes of cavitary lung lesions.
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Nodular pulmonary amyloidosis (case-report level), Behcet disease (pulmonary infarcts/cavities, rare), Tularemia and Sporotrichosis (uncommon cavitation), Radiation and bevacizumab-related cavitation (documented but uncommon), Ankylosing spondylitis (upper-lobe fibrobullous cavities), Scedosporium and Fusarium (immunocompromised case series), EGPA (rarely cavitates). Caplan syndrome, paragonimiasis, Rhodococcus equi and Hyper-IgE syndrome scored as Board Prep Traps.

answers.name: Lung abscess
answers.pearl: A necrotic, pus-filled cavity usually from aspiration of oral anaerobes, classically with an air-fluid level in a dependent segment.

answers.name: Tuberculosis
answers.pearl: Reactivation TB classically cavitates in the apical and posterior upper lobes, often in a patient with weeks of cough, sweats and weight loss.

answers.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
answers.pearl: Squamous histology is the lung cancer type most likely to cavitate because of central tumor necrosis.

answers.name: Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia
answers.pearl: S. aureus, including MRSA, causes necrotizing pneumonia with multiple thin-walled cavities and pneumatoceles, especially after influenza or via hematogenous spread.

answers.name: Klebsiella pneumonia
answers.pearl: Klebsiella causes a necrotizing upper-lobe pneumonia with a bulging fissure and cavitation, typically in alcoholics and diabetics.

answers.name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
answers.pearl: GPA produces multiple nodules that cavitate, with sinus disease and glomerulonephritis, and is PR3-ANCA positive.

answers.name: Septic pulmonary emboli
answers.pearl: Peripheral, multiple nodules at different stages of cavitation suggest septic emboli from tricuspid endocarditis, infected lines, or septic thrombophlebitis.

answers.name: Pulmonary infarction
answers.pearl: A bland pulmonary embolism can infarct a lung segment and occasionally the infarct cavitates, particularly if it becomes infected.

answers.name: Aspiration pneumonia
answers.pearl: Aspiration into dependent segments, such as the posterior upper lobes or superior lower lobes, can progress to necrotizing pneumonia and abscess.

answers.name: Metastatic cancer
answers.pearl: Metastases from squamous primaries such as head and neck or cervical cancer, and from sarcoma, can form cavitary nodules.

answers.name: Histoplasmosis
answers.pearl: Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis mimics TB in older smokers with emphysema and is common in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys.

answers.name: Aspergilloma
answers.pearl: A fungus ball within a preexisting cavity, such as from old TB or sarcoid, shows a mobile mass with an air crescent and can cause hemoptysis.

answers.name: Coccidioidomycosis
answers.pearl: Pulmonary coccidioidomycosis can leave a thin-walled cavity in the southwestern US, which can rupture and cause pneumothorax.

answers.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia
answers.pearl: Pseudomonas causes necrotizing pneumonia with cavitation in hospitalized, ventilated, or structurally lung-diseased patients.

answers.name: Blastomycosis
answers.pearl: Blastomyces can cause mass-like consolidation and cavities with verrucous skin lesions in the Great Lakes and Ohio River regions.

answers.name: Rheumatoid nodules
answers.pearl: Necrobiotic rheumatoid nodules in the lung may cavitate, usually in seropositive men with subcutaneous nodules.

answers.name: Nontuberculous mycobacteria
answers.pearl: MAC and M. abscessus cause fibrocavitary disease in smokers or COPD and nodular bronchiectatic disease in older women.

answers.name: Adenocarcinoma of the lung
answers.pearl: Adenocarcinoma cavitates less often than squamous but can show thick-walled cavitation, particularly with invasive mucinous subtypes.

answers.name: Sarcoidosis
answers.pearl: Necrotizing sarcoid granulomatosis and advanced fibrocystic sarcoid can show cavities and are often colonized by Aspergillus.

answers.name: Invasive aspergillosis
answers.pearl: Neutropenic patients develop nodules with a halo sign that cavitate with an air-crescent sign as neutrophils recover.

answers.name: Nocardiosis
answers.pearl: Nocardia causes cavitary pneumonia in transplant, steroid-treated, or alveolar proteinosis patients and can seed the brain.

answers.name: Lymphoma
answers.pearl: Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, especially after treatment, can produce cavitary lung masses.

answers.name: Cryptococcosis
answers.pearl: Cryptococcus can cause cavitating pulmonary nodules, usually in immunocompromised hosts and sometimes in apparently healthy ones.

answers.name: Lemierre syndrome
answers.pearl: Fusobacterium necrophorum infection of the pharynx leads to internal jugular vein thrombosis and cavitating septic emboli to the lungs.

answers.name: Actinomycosis
answers.pearl: Actinomyces causes a chronic cavitating pneumonia that crosses fissures and may invade the chest wall with sulfur granules.

answers.name: Mucormycosis
answers.pearl: Rhizopus and related molds cause cavitating pneumonia with the reversed halo sign in diabetic ketoacidosis and neutropenia.

answers.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
answers.pearl: PJP can produce thin-walled cysts or pneumatoceles, especially in HIV patients on aerosolized pentamidine, with risk of pneumothorax.

answers.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae serotype 3 pneumonia
answers.pearl: Serotype 3 pneumococcus is notorious for necrotizing pneumonia with cavitation and empyema.

answers.name: Community-associated MRSA necrotizing pneumonia
answers.pearl: PVL-positive USA300 MRSA causes rapidly progressive hemorrhagic necrotizing pneumonia with leukopenia, often after influenza.

answers.name: Legionella pneumonia
answers.pearl: Legionella can cavitate in immunosuppressed hosts, especially transplant recipients on steroids.

answers.name: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
answers.pearl: Adult smokers with pulmonary LCH have upper-lobe nodules that evolve into cavitating nodules and then bizarre-shaped cysts, sparing the costophrenic angles.

answers.name: Silicosis
answers.pearl: Progressive massive fibrosis in silicosis can cavitate, often from superimposed tuberculosis, which silica exposure strongly predisposes to.

answers.name: Mycobacterium kansasii
answers.pearl: Kansasii mimics TB with upper-lobe thin-walled cavities in middle-aged men with underlying COPD.

answers.name: Traumatic pulmonary pseudocyst
answers.pearl: Blunt chest trauma can produce a thin-walled traumatic pneumatocele or hematoma-filled cavity that develops hours to days after contusion.

answers.name: Melioidosis
answers.pearl: Burkholderia pseudomallei causes cavitary upper-lobe pneumonia mimicking TB in diabetics in Southeast Asia and northern Australia.

answers.name: Echinococcosis
answers.pearl: A ruptured hydatid cyst gives a cavity with the water lily sign or crescent sign in patients from sheep-raising regions.

answers.name: Amebic lung abscess
aliases: hepatic amebic abscess with lung extension
answers.pearl: Entamoeba histolytica reaches the right lower lung by direct extension through the diaphragm from an amebic liver abscess, producing anchovy-paste sputum.

answers.name: Infected bronchogenic cyst
answers.pearl: Congenital bronchogenic cysts can become infected and communicate with the airway, appearing as an air-fluid-level cavity.

answers.name: Pulmonary sequestration
answers.pearl: An infected intralobar sequestration, usually in the left lower lobe with systemic arterial supply, can appear as a recurrent cavity.

answers.name: Sporotrichosis
answers.pearl: Pulmonary Sporothrix schenckii is an uncommon cause of chronic upper-lobe cavitation, mainly in alcoholics and COPD patients.

answers.name: Paracoccidioidomycosis
answers.pearl: South American blastomycosis causes chronic multifocal lung disease with cavities in rural workers from Brazil and neighboring countries.

answers.name: Cavitation from radiation therapy
answers.pearl: Stereotactic or conventional radiation can cause late cavitation of the irradiated tumor or lung, sometimes with Aspergillus colonization.

answers.name: Bevacizumab-associated tumor cavitation
answers.pearl: Anti-VEGF therapy in squamous lung cancer can cause tumor cavitation with life-threatening hemoptysis.

answers.name: Ankylosing spondylitis
answers.pearl: Late fibrobullous apical disease in ankylosing spondylitis forms upper-lobe cavities that are frequently colonized by Aspergillus.

answers.name: Chronic granulomatous disease
answers.pearl: CGD causes pneumonias from catalase-positive organisms such as Aspergillus, Nocardia and Burkholderia cepacia that may cavitate.

answers.name: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis
answers.pearl: An EBV-driven angiocentric B-cell lymphoproliferation causing bilateral lower-lobe nodules that cavitate and may involve skin and CNS.

answers.name: Talaromycosis
answers.pearl: Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei causes disseminated disease with cavitation in HIV patients from or travelling to Southeast Asia.

answers.name: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
answers.pearl: EGPA seldom cavitates, but cavitating nodules in the setting of asthma and eosinophilia have been reported.

answers.name: Pulmonary angiosarcoma metastases
answers.pearl: Metastatic angiosarcoma and other sarcomas produce thin-walled cavitating nodules that can cause recurrent pneumothorax.

answers.name: Scedosporium infection
answers.pearl: Scedosporium apiospermum causes cavitary pneumonia indistinguishable from aspergillosis, in transplant patients and near-drowning victims, and is resistant to amphotericin.

answers.name: Fusarium pneumonia
answers.pearl: Angioinvasive Fusarium in neutropenic patients can cavitate and often coexists with positive blood cultures and necrotic skin lesions.

answers.name: Behcet disease
answers.pearl: Pulmonary artery aneurysms and thrombosis in Behcet disease can produce infarcts that cavitate, and anticoagulation is hazardous.

answers.name: Tularemia
answers.pearl: Francisella tularensis pneumonia from inhaling contaminated dust or handling infected rabbits may cavitate if untreated.

answers.name: Nodular pulmonary amyloidosis
answers.pearl: Rarely, localized nodular amyloid deposits in the lung can cavitate, especially with underlying MALT lymphoma or Sjogren syndrome.

answers.name: Caplan syndrome
answers.pearl: Rheumatoid arthritis plus pneumoconiosis (classically coal) gives multiple well-defined, peripheral, often cavitating nodules.

answers.name: Paragonimiasis
answers.pearl: Eating raw freshwater crab or crayfish with Paragonimus westermani causes cavitary or cystic lung disease with rusty brown sputum that mimics TB.

answers.name: Rhodococcus equi pneumonia
answers.pearl: Cavitary pneumonia in an immunosuppressed host, classically with advanced HIV or transplant, who has contact with horses or soil.

answers.name: Hyper-IgE syndrome
answers.pearl: STAT3 hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome leads to staphylococcal pneumonias that heal with persistent pneumatoceles prone to Aspergillus infection.

prompts.prompt: Name causes of fever with rash in an adult.
prompts.review_notes: Least sure: Cryptococcosis and Disseminated candidiasis (skin lesions uncommon), Strongyloides hyperinfection (periumbilical purpura, case-series level), Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes and Schnitzler syndrome (urticarial rash with fever, rare), Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma and Intravascular lymphoma (rash inconsistent), Kikuchi disease (rash in minority), Atypical measles, Smallpox (eradicated; historical/bioterror), Anaplasmosis (rash uncommon), Capnocytophaga. RMSF, Kawasaki disease, typhoid fever and acute rheumatic fever scored as Board Prep Traps.

answers.name: Viral exanthem
answers.pearl: Nonspecific viral infections (enterovirus, adenovirus, echovirus) commonly cause a fever with a diffuse maculopapular rash that resolves on its own.
